title: Shared Values Counted With Repeats
statement:
You get two integer arrays a and b. Return their common values, keeping repeats: a value that appears x times in a and y times in b appears min(x, y) times in the answer.

The answer may be in any order.

examples.why: 4 appears twice in a and three times in b, so it is shared twice. Removing duplicates would give only one 4.
2 is shared once (b has one), 3 is shared once (a has one).

hints: A set loses how many times each value appears. What would remember the count?
Count the values of one array in a hash map. Then walk the other array and use up those counts.
For each value in b, if its count in the map is still positive, add it to the answer and decrease the count.

explain.intuition:
The twist compared with a plain set intersection is that repeats matter, so you need counts, not membership. Count every value in a. Then each value in b can "claim" one remaining copy from a. Once a value's count reaches zero, further copies in b have no partner.

If both arrays are already sorted, two pointers do the same job with no map: move the pointer at the smaller value forward, and on equal values take one and move both.
steps: Build count: how many times each value appears in a.
Walk b. For each value v with count[v] > 0, push v and decrease count[v].
pitfalls: Using a set, which reports a shared value once no matter how many copies both arrays have.
Adding a value every time it appears in b, without decreasing the count. That returns max copies instead of min.
Counting the larger array when memory is tight. Counting the smaller one keeps the map small.

complexity.space: O(min(n, m)) if you count the smaller array

solutions.title: Find and cross off
solutions.idea: For each value in a, search a working copy of b for an unused equal value and cross it off.

solutions.title: Count one side, spend from the other
solutions.idea: Count the values of a in a map. Each value of b uses up one copy if any are left.

solutions.title: Sort both and walk two pointers
solutions.idea: After sorting, advance the pointer at the smaller value; on a match take it and advance both.
solutions.time: O(n log n + m log m)

followups: What if both arrays are already sorted? Which solution would you pick then?
b is too big for memory and arrives in chunks from disk. How do you still compute the answer?
